purpose: The estate's recorded position on the governance SharePoint lists: what is known to diverge between the specification, the live tenant, and the flows that consume them. tests/governance-estate.test.mjs asserts the live evidence against this file, so the divergence stays visible and cannot silently widen or be silently fixed without the record moving with it.

evidence.governanceFlowPackages: docs/reference/flow-contracts/deployed/ — the eight 0N-GOV-* definitions, imported from Paxkages_updated_Governance.zip (packages dated 2026-09-08/09)
evidence.listRegistry: docs/reference/governance-list-registry.json — the authoritative instance per list, and the 17 to retire
evidence.flowCorrections: docs/deployment/governance/flows/ — corrected definitions for the four HTTP flows
evidence.provisioningRun: Executed 2026-09-09 against DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE: dry run, apply, and two verification re-runs.

endpointImpact.note: CORRECTED 2026-09-09. This previously read `newContractKeys: 0` with the note that the governance structure introduced no HTTP endpoint at all. That was true of the earlier snapshot, where every governance flow was a button-triggered provisioning scope. The updated packages are not: four of the eight declare an HTTP POST trigger with triggerAuthenticationType All — anonymous, authenticated only by the SAS signature in the URL, the same posture as the estate's other 25. They add no CONTRACT KEY, because neither delivered platform calls them: they are machine-to-machine governance intake, called by other flows and by registering systems. But they are endpoints, they carry signatures, and they belong in the rotation scope and in any inventory that claims to cover the estate. The 25 contract keys across 20 workflows are unchanged.
endpointImpact.consequence: Whoever holds one of these four URLs can write to the governance registry anonymously. GOV-05 records what the retirement endpoint does with that.

openFindings.title: Governance lists: one authoritative site, provisioned and verified; the registry lists remain
openFindings.detail: The specification and the consumers named different site collections: sharepoint-provisioning-spec.json targeted NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING while the internal flows address DGO_UserDirectory, DGO_RoleCatalogue and DGO_AuditLog by GUID on DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE. That divergence is CLOSED: the specification now targets DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE for all ten lists, by GUID, and divergentLists is empty because nothing diverges any more. What remains is execution — the tenant has not been provisioned from the corrected specification, so the governance features still do not work.
openFindings.resolution: Run docs/deployment/governance/GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 2 (scripts/provision-governance-lists.browser.js, dry run then apply then verify). Then re-capture the tenant list index and close this finding.
openFindings.owner: Platform technical owner, with the tenant administrator
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block the endpoint commissioning path — that reaches Power Automate directly and touches no governance list. It blocks the governance features: enrolment, the role catalogue, and the audit trail landing where anything reads it.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: RESOLVED IN THE REPOSITORY. sharepoint-provisioning-spec.json now targets DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE for all ten lists, addressed by GUID, applied by scripts/repoint-governance-provisioning.mjs and held by npm run test:governancerepoint.
openFindings.tenantStatus: STEP 2 COMPLETE AND VERIFIED IDEMPOTENT, 2026-09-09. Three consecutive runs of scripts/provision-governance-lists.browser.js against DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE: dry run 0 created / 97 present / 0 failed; apply 1 created (EndpointRedacted) / 97 present / 0 failed; verify 0 created / 98 present / 10 seeds present / 0 failed. All ten lists carry every column and seed row the specification declares, addressed by GUID on the single authoritative site. The '97 of 97 present' of the first run — which counted a column that did not exist — is superseded by a report that means what it says. Steps 3 to 6 remain.

openFindings.title: Every governance list existed two or three times; the 17 duplicates are now renamed, not yet deleted
openFindings.detail: The 2026-08-18 capture shows all ten governance lists on both DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE and NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING, and seven of them additionally carrying a _2 copy on NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING. A _2 suffix is SharePoint disambiguating a title that already existed, which is the signature of a title-based provisioning flow run more than once or run against the wrong site. A flow writing DGO_AuditLog and one reading DGO_AuditLog_2 both succeed and neither sees the other.
openFindings.rootCause: The governance provisioning path creates by title against _api/web/lists. The portal path was deliberately hardened against exactly this — docs/deployment/sharepoint/portal-field-spec.json addresses every list by GUID so that, in its own words, a typo can never produce a duplicate list — and the governance path did not inherit the fix.
openFindings.resolution: Decide which instance of each list is authoritative (the ones the internal flows address by GUID are the ones in use), retire the others, and move the governance provisioning path onto GUID addressing before it is run again. Then re-capture and update this record.
openFindings.owner: Tenant administrator, with the platform technical owner
openFindings.blocksNote: As GOV-01: the endpoint commissioning path is unaffected.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: ROOT CAUSE RESOLVED IN THE REPOSITORY. Every governance address is now a list GUID, so re-running provisioning cannot mint a further copy. scripts/provision-governance-lists.browser.js replaces the title-based flow path entirely.
openFindings.tenantStatus: OUTSTANDING, AND NOT YET SAFE TO DELETE. The 17 duplicate instances still exist. The survey of 2026-09-09 found four of them written at 2026-08-31, after the audit capture — see GOV-09. Step 3's survey, export and rename phases are safe and should proceed; the rename is what will make the producer fail loudly. The DELETE phase is gated on GOV-09: the deployed flows create lists by title, so deleting before the producer is corrected recreates the duplicates on its next run.

openFindings.title: DGO_EndpointRegistry.FlowUrl would hold a signed trigger URL
openFindings.detail: The list DGO_EndpointRegistry declares FlowUrl as a required Note field for the Power Automate endpoint URL. A signed trigger URL is a bearer credential: possession alone authorises invoking the flow, so a list field holding one hands every reader of that list every endpoint. SharePoint list read access is ordinarily far wider than Power Automate maker access. The newer HTTP flow registry gets this right — DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry stores EndpointRedacted and EndpointFingerprint, never the raw URL — so the correct design already exists in the estate and this list predates it.
openFindings.observed: The provisioning flow seeds FlowUrl as an empty string, so no signature is written by the specified path today. The field is required, which means anything that does write a row must supply one.
openFindings.resolution: Bring DGO_EndpointRegistry onto the same design as DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry: a redacted endpoint plus a fingerprint, and no field that can hold a signature. Until then, write no signed URL into it.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: RESOLVED IN THE REPOSITORY. scripts/correct-governance-fields.mjs renames DGO_EndpointRegistry.FlowUrl to EndpointRedacted — the endpoint with its query string removed, so it cannot carry a sig — and adds an EndpointFingerprint Text column, bringing the list onto the DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry design. Held by npm run test:governancefields.
openFindings.tenantStatus: COLUMN DESIGN DONE; FlowUrl RETIREMENT OUTSTANDING. DGO_EndpointRegistry now carries EndpointRedacted (created 2026-09-09, correct internal name) and EndpointFingerprint. The list is on the DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry design. FlowUrl itself remains: empty on all 6 rows, no signature in any of them, so no credential is exposed and nothing needs revoking. Retiring it is GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md 2.8 and is deliberately not urgent — the deployed flow 'Repair the DGO governance lists' creates FlowUrl from its own SchemaXml and will restore the column, so the flow correction in Step 4 should land first or the deletion is undone.

openFindings.title: None of the four HTTP governance endpoints returns an outcome to its caller
openFindings.detail: 02, 03 and 07 declare no Response action at all. 05 declares one — `Reply` — but it runs after `Scope_05_GOV_Retire_HTTP_Flow_COMPLETE_UPDATED`, and every path through that scope ends in a Terminate, so `Reply` is unreachable. In all four cases the caller receives Power Automate's default acknowledgement and never learns what happened. Worse, the validation failures terminate with runStatus Failed AFTER the trigger has already accepted the request, so a caller that submits an invalid registration, an unrecorded execution, or a retirement of a flow that is not in the registry sees the same acknowledgement as one that succeeded.
openFindings.consequence: A registering system cannot tell registration from rejection, so the registry silently under-records and the ledger silently drops executions. This is the same failure the portal's V-02 finding fixed on the citizen side: reporting acceptance for something that was not accepted.
openFindings.resolution: Give each of the four a Response action on every path — success and each Terminate branch — carrying the estate's response envelope, and place it before the Terminate rather than after the scope. For 05, move `Reply` inside the scope ahead of the terminations, or drop it: unreachable code that looks like a reply is worse than none.
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block the endpoint commissioning path. It makes the governance registry unreliable from the moment it is used.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: CORRECTED DEFINITIONS PRODUCED. docs/deployment/governance/flows/*.corrected.json add a reachable Response before every Terminate on all four flows — 15 responses in total. Reachability, status/runStatus agreement and body determinism are asserted by tests/governance-flow-corrections.test.mjs.
openFindings.tenantStatus: OUTSTANDING. The deployed flows are unchanged until GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4 is applied.

openFindings.title: The retirement endpoint cascades unconditionally, and anyone holding its URL can call it
openFindings.detail: 05 - GOV - Retire HTTP Flow accepts an anonymous POST of {environmentId, flowId, retirementReason} — triggerAuthenticationType All, so the SAS signature in the URL is the whole of the authentication. It then retires the registry row, closes every current contract version, and marks every non-retired consumer and every non-retired dependency as Retired, before resolving the flow's open exceptions. The workbook's own key control for this scenario reads: 'verify no active consumers/dependencies remain' and 'stop new traffic before technical removal'. The flow does not verify. It retires them, which erases the evidence that any were active.
openFindings.consequence: One request removes a flow's governance record and every relationship recorded against it, and — per GOV-04 — returns no body saying what it removed. There is no approval step, no dry run, and no way for the caller to discover the blast radius before or after.
openFindings.resolution: Implement the documented control: count active consumers and dependencies first and refuse the retirement when any exist, returning them to the caller so the owner can act. Keep the cascade behind an explicit force flag that is recorded on the registry row. Consider whether an operation this destructive should be anonymous at all — Tenant authentication is available and is what IP_SCAN_INTAKE already uses.
openFindings.owner: Platform technical owner, with the governance owner for the approval decision
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block the endpoint commissioning path, and it is not live until the seven registry lists are provisioned. It should be resolved before they are.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: CORRECTED DEFINITION PRODUCED. The cascade is gated by If_Safe_To_Retire: both active counts are taken before any write, retirement is blocked with 409 when either is non-zero, and proceeds only when both are zero or force is true. Retire_Registry was lifted out of If_Registry_Found, where it would otherwise have escaped the guard — a defect the test found, not the design. A forced retirement is recorded with both counts.
openFindings.tenantStatus: OUTSTANDING. GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4.3 validates all four paths against the live flow.

openFindings.title: The exported flow definitions and the tenant register cannot be joined
openFindings.detail: The repository holds 77 exported flow definitions, each identified by a 36-character Power Automate flow GUID. The register holds 51 workflow records, each identified by a 32-hex Logic Apps workflow id. These are different identifier spaces for the same objects, and ZERO exported definitions carry an id the register knows. Joining on normalised display name — the only field the two share — matches 13. That leaves 64 exported definitions the register does not name and 37 register workflows for which no definition is held, with 1 name reused across records.
openFindings.consequence: Nobody can answer 'is this exported flow one of the 51?' — so any statement comparing the two counts is comparing populations measured on different axes. This audit made that mistake: an earlier recommendation set '77 exported definitions' against '51 tenant workflows' as though one contained the other. It does not, and the overlap is 13.
openFindings.resolution: Record both identifiers in one place. DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry is designed to do exactly this — FlowId alongside RegistryKey, written once at registration — which is the strongest single argument for adopting it. Until then, npm run reconcile:definitions maintains the name-based map and states its own limits, and tests/governance-estate.test.mjs holds the numbers so the gap cannot be quoted wrongly again.
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block commissioning. It blocks any claim about the size or coverage of the flow estate.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: BLOCKERS 1 AND 2 CLOSED, 2026-09-10. WorkflowId is in the registry specification (scripts/lib/registry-spec-amendments.mjs, applied by the extractor so the JSON stays derived), and flow 02 accepts `workflowId` on its trigger, refuses a dashed 36-character flowId with 400, and writes the value on both arms of the registry upsert. Blockers 3 and 4 are not defects and cannot be closed: only 56 of 77 exported definitions carry an HTTP trigger, and idOverlap is ceilinged at 51. scripts/reconcile-flow-definitions.mjs still maintains the name-based map and states its limits.
openFindings.tenantStatus: OUTSTANDING. Nothing has been provisioned or applied. Step 5.3a creates the column; Step 4 applies the corrected flow 02; Step 6 populates the join. NOTE: flow 01's Compose_Final_Report_JSON.validation.expectedFields and the configuration seed ProvisioningSchemaExpectedFieldCount both still state 101. Provisioning 102 columns without updating them makes flow 01 report a variance against a correct run.

openFindings.title: A live producer wrote seed rows to the NON-authoritative site thirteen days after the audit
openFindings.detail: The Step 3 survey of 2026-09-09 read all 17 duplicate list instances on NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING. Thirteen are empty. Four carry items: DGO_AuditLog 5, DGO_RoleCatalogue 6, DGO_UserDirectory 1, DGO_PilotCohorts 1. All four report LastItemModifiedDate 2026-08-31T01:58:48-49Z — within one second of each other, which is one run, not four accidents. The list capture this estate reasons from is dated 2026-08-18, so the write happened THIRTEEN DAYS AFTER the audit that recorded these lists as duplicates to retire.
openFindings.evidence: The row counts match the specification's seed set exactly: 6 role seeds, 1 bootstrap user, 1 pilot cohort. That is a provisioning run, and it was pointed at the non-authoritative site.
openFindings.consequence: Step 3's delete phase cannot be executed until the producer is known. Deleting a list nothing writes to is housekeeping; deleting a list something still writes to breaks that producer silently.
openFindings.resolution: Two things, in order. First, scripts/compare-duplicate-governance-lists.browser.js answers whether any row exists ONLY in a duplicate — if one does, it is the sole copy and must be reconciled before any deletion. Second, find and correct the producer, which is Step 4 work: nothing readable from a list says what wrote to it. Only then does Step 3's delete phase become safe. Step 3's survey, export and rename phases are unaffected and should proceed — the rename is precisely what makes a live producer fail loudly while the fix is still one restore away.
openFindings.owner: Platform technical owner, with the governance owner for the flow correction
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block the endpoint commissioning path, which touches no governance list. It blocks the DELETE phase of Step 3, and it re-orders the runbook: Step 4 before Step 3.4.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: MEASURED AND TOOLED. scripts/build-governance-comparison.mjs emits a read-only row-by-row comparison of every duplicate against the instance that supersedes it, keyed on the list's own seed key field rather than Title — two of these lists legitimately repeat titles. Nine duplicates declare no key field; all nine are empty, and the script reports CANNOT COMPARE rather than guessing at row identity.
openFindings.tenantStatus: SURVEY, EXPORT AND RENAME COMPLETE, 2026-09-09. All 17 duplicates exported (13 items in total: DGO_AuditLog 5, DGO_RoleCatalogue 6, DGO_UserDirectory 1, DGO_PilotCohorts 1; 0 failed) and all 17 renamed to ZZ_RETIRED_* (0 failed). The rename has already had its intended effect on one known hazard: every deployed reference to these lists is by title, so ZZ_RETIRED_ makes those calls 404 rather than silently hit a duplicate. DELETE remains blocked until the producer of the 2026-08-31 rows is identified in the tenant.
openFindings.correction: An earlier version of this finding asserted that the deployed flows create these lists BY TITLE and would recreate the duplicates on their next run. That was carried over from the GOV-02 narrative and was NOT checked against the definitions. It is wrong. Every exported definition naming a governance list was walked: NONE creates a list, and NONE posts an item to one. The claim has been withdrawn rather than softened.

producerSearch.corpusSearched: every exported definition under docs/reference/flow-contracts/deployed that names a governance list
producerSearch.conclusion: The producer of the 13 seed rows is NOT in the exported corpus. That is consistent with GOV-06: the exports and the tenant register share no identifier and only 13 of 73 exported definitions match a register workflow by name, so the corpus is known to be partial. The producer is unidentified, not absent.
producerSearch.nextProbe: The tenant, not the repository: Power Automate run history for 2026-08-31 01:58 UTC in environment Default-ca6a4b3f-9123-49bc-bcb9-27085ebbf1a1, or the SharePoint audit log for the four lists at that timestamp. Nothing readable from a list says what wrote to it.

openFindings.title: The 'Repair the DGO governance lists' flow is hardcoded to the non-authoritative site and deletes columns it does not recognise
openFindings.detail: Flow bc095fa2-28a4-4312-9076-87caac5ca116, button-triggered. Every one of its six actions carries dataset = https://nitdanigeria.sharepoint.com/sites/NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING — the site whose lists are being retired — and every one addresses its list by getbytitle('...'), never by GUID. It creates and indexes columns, and it DELETES any column its Filter_Strays step does not recognise.
openFindings.evidence: Its SchemaXml payload carries FlowUrl and ScopeId — the exact two names GOV-03 and GOV-08 removed — and does NOT carry EndpointRedacted or EndpointFingerprint. It does carry AccessScopeId, so it has been partially updated by hand at some point.
openFindings.consequence: If this flow is ever repointed at DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE, or if the retired lists are restored to their original titles, it will classify EndpointRedacted and EndpointFingerprint as strays and DELETE them, then recreate FlowUrl and ScopeId — undoing GOV-03 and GOV-08 in a single button press, and reporting success while doing it. It writes no items, so it is not the GOV-09 producer.
openFindings.resolution: Correct it in Step 4 alongside the other flow work: repoint dataset to the authoritative site, address lists by GUID rather than getbytitle, and regenerate its varLists payload from docs/reference/sharepoint-provisioning-spec.json so the column set it enforces is the corrected one. Until then it should not be run. Its title-addressing is currently harmless only because the duplicates are renamed — that is a side effect of Step 3, not a control.
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block commissioning. It is a live undo button for GOV-03 and GOV-08, and it is one click away.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: MEASURED. The definition is held and its dataset, addressing mode and SchemaXml payload are read directly from it.
openFindings.tenantStatus: OUTSTANDING. The flow is deployed and runnable as it stands.

openFindings.title: A parallel flow-truth database was provisioned outside the specification, by title, on an unrecorded site, without the internal-name hint
openFindings.detail: Two browser scripts — NITDA_Flow_Truth_SharePoint_Provisioning_BROWSER_CONSOLE1.js and NITDA_Flow_Truth_SharePoint_Provisioning_RESUME_FIX.js — were reported executed against the tenant on 2026-09-10. Between them they create two lists and one document library titled 'NITDA Flow Truth Registry', 'NITDA Flow Truth History' and 'NITDA Flow Truth Artefacts', with 37, 37 and 16 columns respectively (90 column creations), five views, three folders, and uniqueness enforced on RegistryKey and HistoryKey. None of the three appears in docs/reference/http-flow-registry-spec.json, sharepoint-provisioning-spec.json, portal-field-spec.json, internal-field-evidence.json, or the 326-list capture of 2026-08-18.

evidence.noSitePin: Both scripts set siteUrl from window._spPageContextInfo.webAbsoluteUrl, falling back to location.origin + the path before /SitePages/. The target is whichever page the console happened to be open on. GOV-01 made .../sites/DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE authoritative and GOV-09 records a producer writing to .../sites/NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING; nothing in either script can distinguish them, and neither writes the site it used anywhere durable. The only record is window.NITDA_FLOW_TRUTH_PROVISIONING_RESULT.siteUrl, which lives in that browser session and nowhere else.
evidence.titleAddressing: Every list, library, field, view and folder operation in both scripts is addressed by web/lists/GetByTitle('...'). This is the operation that produced GOV-02, in which every governance list existed two or three times.
evidence.optionsZero: createfieldasxml is called with Options: 0. The estate's own provisioners call it with Options: 24, and 8 of that is AddFieldInternalNameHint — the bit that makes SharePoint take the internal name from the SchemaXml Name attribute rather than deriving it from the display name. Without bit 8 a column declared Name="RegistryKey" DisplayName="Registry Key" is not guaranteed to receive the internal name RegistryKey. Bit 16, AddFieldToDefaultView, is also absent, so no created column is added to the default view.
evidence.idempotenceDependsOnTheAbsentBit: CONSOLE1's guard is existing.has(definition.internalName), where existing is a Set of InternalName read back from the list and definition.internalName is the SchemaXml Name. That comparison is only sound when bit 8 is set. If SharePoint derived the internal names, the guard never matches, every re-run re-creates every column, and SharePoint auto-disambiguates by appending a digit — the exact pathology cleanup-disambiguated-columns.browser.js was built for.
evidence.theFirstRunDidNotComplete: CONSOLE1 creates views by POSTing SP.View to web/lists/GetByTitle('...')/views with ViewFields as a Collection(Edm.String). RESUME_FIX replaces exactly that call with views/add and SP.ViewCreationInformation. The existence and content of RESUME_FIX is evidence that CONSOLE1 did not run to completion: view creation precedes folder creation in CONSOLE1, and RESUME_FIX creates the folders.
evidence.resumeFixClearsRequired: RESUME_FIX's index() sends { Indexed: true, EnforceUniqueValues: unique, Required: unique } on every call. Fifteen of its eighteen calls pass unique=false, so they send Required: false — clearing the Required flag CONSOLE1 set on EnvironmentId and FlowId, which it declared Required="TRUE".
evidence.assertsWhatItDoesNotEnforce: CredentialsExcluded and ContainsSensitiveData are Boolean columns defaulting to 1. S1 of docs/audits/FLOW_TRUTH_PERSISTENCE_REVIEW.md records that the record written to these lists carries the flow's own trigger URL and sig= token. A column that asserts credentials are excluded, defaulted true, on a row that carries one, is a false assurance in the schema itself.
evidence.librarySpacesUnresolved: C9 of the same review records that the artefact URLs are built by concatenating an unencoded server-relative Path containing the library title. 'NITDA Flow Truth Artefacts' contains three spaces. Provisioning the library under that title does not resolve C9; it commits the estate to it.

openFindings.consequence: The estate now has, or may have, a second implementation of the flow-truth database beside the one it specifies: 3 resources and 90 columns provisioned ad hoc, against 7 lists and 101 fields specified and guarded. Two implementations of one capability is the condition GOV-02 describes at list level — a writer populating one while a reader queries the other, both succeeding, neither seeing the other. Because the site was never pinned or recorded, the repository cannot say which site received it, so it cannot say whether GOV-01's authoritative site now carries unspecified lists or whether the non-authoritative site does. B1 of the flow-truth review is measured against the 2026-08-18 capture and is therefore no longer a statement about the live tenant.
openFindings.resolution: Do not run either script again — a re-run is the duplication case, not a repair. Run the read-only scripts/verify-flow-truth-provisioning.browser.js on BOTH sites to establish what exists, on which site, under which internal names, and how many disambiguated copies. Only then decide between adopting the three resources into http-flow-registry-spec.json and retiring them in favour of the specified seven lists. Both are agency decisions; neither is the executing agent's to make.
openFindings.blocksNote: It does not block commissioning: nothing in the commissioning path reads these three resources, and the designer package that would write to them does not save (B1–B7). It is recorded because it is unmeasured tenant state created outside the specification, and because the next re-run duplicates it.
openFindings.repositoryStatus: MEASURED against the scripts themselves. Every claim above is read from the two files; none is read from the tenant.
openFindings.tenantStatus: UNMEASURED. Execution is reported, not observed. Whether the resources exist, on which site, and under which internal names is unknown until scripts/verify-flow-truth-provisioning.browser.js is run.

closedFindings.title: The seven HTTP flow registry lists are specified but not provisioned
closedFindings.detail: docs/reference/http-flow-registry-spec.json declares 7 lists and 101 fields on DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE and states that none is provisioned. The 2026-08-18 capture confirms all seven are absent. Specification and reality agree; nothing is outstanding until the provisioning flow is run.

closedFindings.title: DGO_AccessScopes appeared damaged in the tenant
closedFindings.detail: Recorded from the live run of 2026-09-09 as a damaged list, on the evidence that its columns read back while every operation touching its item store returned 500. That diagnosis was wrong. The list loads normally in the browser. The cause is GOV-08: ScopeId is a SharePoint reserved field name, the presence check matched the system field, and both failing operations were being performed against that system field rather than against a column the specification owns.

closedFindings.title: One specification column used a name SharePoint reserves, and was reported present against its own system field
closedFindings.detail: ScopeId is a SharePoint system field: every list carries a hidden one holding the item's security scope. The specification declares a custom Text column of the same name on DGO_AccessScopes, so the provisioner's presence check answered yes against SharePoint's field, reported the column present, and never created the specification's. Both subsequent operations then failed — indexing a system field returns 500 'Cannot complete this action.', and filtering a Guid-typed system field against the string 'all' returns 500 'List does not exist. It may have been deleted by another user.' That is the whole of GOV-07: not a damaged list, a reserved name.
closedFindings.evidence: The list loads normally in the browser and its view shows a column titled 'Access Scope Id' — the tenant's actual custom column. Two further names were added to this finding by generalisation rather than observation, and the tenant disproved both: Version is an ordinary custom column on each list, populated and working. SharePoint's own version field is _UIVersionString.
closedFindings.consequence: The live run of 2026-09-09 reported 97 of 97 columns present. One of those was a false positive. The over-generalisation then cost more than the original defect: it renamed two working columns in the specification, and the run created Version0 and FlowUrl0 beside the originals — three empty columns SharePoint auto-disambiguated, which now have to be removed.
closedFindings.resolution: Confirm each of the three against the tenant, then rename them in the specification to names SharePoint does not reserve — AccessScopeId, CatalogueVersion, EndpointVersion are the obvious candidates — and re-run the provisioner so the real columns are created. Where a custom column already holds the data under another name, adopt that name rather than creating a second.
closedFindings.owner: Platform technical owner, with the tenant administrator
closedFindings.blocksNote: It does not block the endpoint commissioning path. It blocks trusting the provisioning report: 97 of 97 present was not 97 of 97 present.
closedFindings.repositoryStatus: RESOLVED IN THE REPOSITORY. scripts/correct-governance-fields.mjs renames ScopeId to AccessScopeId and WITHDRAWS the two Version renames, restoring the field, its SchemaXml and its seed payloads. 'Version' is out of the reserved-name list in tests/governance-estate.test.mjs, with the reason recorded there: a name belongs in that list because it was observed to collide, never because it resembles one that did — a false entry forces a rename, and renaming a populated column is a data migration.
closedFindings.tenantStatus: RESOLVED IN THE TENANT. DGO_AccessScopes.AccessScopeId carries the intended internal name, is indexed, and the seed AccessScopeId='all' is written — the 500s that were first misrecorded as GOV-07 are gone. The three columns SharePoint auto-disambiguated on 2026-09-09 were deleted on the same date by scripts/cleanup-disambiguated-columns.browser.js: a dry run listed exactly DGO_EndpointRegistry.FlowUrl0, DGO_EndpointRegistry.Version0 and DGO_RoleCatalogue.Version0, and the live run reported 3 deleted, 0 kept because they hold data, 0 failed. Both original Version columns are untouched and still populated — 'R11.6-PILOT' on six role rows, 'document-portal.1' on six registry rows. No data was lost at any point.
withdrawn: DGO_RoleCatalogue.Version — kept. FromBaseType=false, CanBeDeleted=true, 6 of 6 rows populated with 'R11.6-PILOT'. Never a collision.
DGO_EndpointRegistry.Version — kept. Same flags, 6 of 6 rows populated with 'document-portal.1'. Never a collision.
